text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Public brand site + product catalogue + technical resource centre + lead engine, modelled on williamsrefrigeration.co.in. Owner: platform eng Rev 1.0 2026-10-07

Design stance: this is a read-heavy, low-write, SEO-critical B2B site. The scaling risk is NOT queries per second — it is content velocity, crawlability and never dropping an enquiry. So: cheap and boring today, with the seams pre-cut where the next 10x actually lands.

text.tspan: 2 · The two paths that must not break

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Everything else on this page can degrade. These two define the business.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: A · Lead capture — zero tolerance for a dropped enquiry

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: 1 POST /v1/leads with Idempotency-Key (collapses double-clicks + client retries)
2 Edge: Turnstile score + honeypot + time-to-fill + per-IP Redis bucket
3 Validate, normalise phone/email, hash the IP (abuse only, never stored raw)
4 ONE Postgres transaction: INSERT lead + INSERT lead_item[] + INSERT outbox('lead.created')
5 Respond 202 with lead_ref — the user sees success in under 300 ms
6 Worker drains outbox -> email to sales + ack to customer + CRM upsert + WhatsApp ping
7 CRM or mail provider down? The row stays in outbox. Exponential retry, then DLQ + page.
WHY: the database commit is the durability boundary, and no third party sits on the
user's request path. A SaaS outage delays notification; it never loses the lead.
Verification: a synthetic lead is submitted every 5 minutes end to end, and an alert
fires on zero real leads during a business hour — silent form failure is the expensive bug.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: B · Publish — editor click to live page, p95 under 30 s

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: 1 Editor saves -> content_revision row (draft, full JSONB snapshot); media via signed PUT to S3
2 Publish -> txn: UPDATE product SET status='live', version=version+1 + outbox('catalog.changed')
3 Indexer bulk-upserts the changed documents into OpenSearch (1 s debounce)
4 Purge worker: CDN surrogate-key purge + Next.js revalidateTag('product:<id>')
5 Sitemap diff regenerated per locale, IndexNow ping to Google and Bing
6 Rollback = publish the previous revision. No deploy, no DBA, no downtime.
WHY tag-based purge and not a wildcard: a spec correction on one SKU must not cold-start
the whole catalogue and hand every visitor an origin round-trip. Each rendered page
declares the entity tags it read, so invalidation is exactly as wide as the change.
WHY a revision snapshot and not a diff: at ~20 publishes a week the storage is free and
'restore exactly what was live on the day of the trade show' becomes a one-row operation.

text.tspan: Key modelling decisions (the ones that get argued about in review)

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: 1 Hybrid relational + JSONB, deliberately — not one or the other.
The skeleton (category -> product -> variant -> asset -> document, plus the product<->industry m:n)
is a fixed graph with real integrity rules, so it is relational with enforced foreign keys. The spec
sheet is not fixed: a blast freezer has pull-down time, a wine chiller has bottle count, a serve-over
has pane geometry. Those live in product.specs / variant.dims_mm as JSONB behind a GIN index, with a
per-category JSON Schema validating them on write. A new product family therefore ships with zero
migration, while foreign keys still make orphaned variants and assets impossible.
2 The VARIANT, not the product, is the unit of truth for specs.
Williams shows one 'Blast Freezer' page but sells many model codes. Dimensions, capacity, energy class
and price belong to the SKU; marketing copy belongs to the product. Collapsing the two is the single
mistake that forces a schema rewrite in year two, the moment someone asks for a price list.
3 Bytes never go in the database. asset holds metadata plus a storage_key; S3 holds the file; the CDN
serves it. This keeps the Postgres working set in RAM and keeps restores measured in minutes.
4 Content is versioned; demand is immutable. content_revision keeps a full JSONB snapshot per publish.
lead and application rows are never edited in place — status transitions append to audit_log, which is
how you answer 'who touched this enquiry, and when' during a commission dispute.
5 Derived stores are disposable. OpenSearch, Redis and ClickHouse can all be dropped and rebuilt from
Postgres. Nothing is stored only in them. That rule is what keeps one backup and one restore drill.
6 Indexes come from the actual query shapes, not from habit:
GiST on category.path (subtree reads) and on installation.geo (radius search)
GIN on product.specs (containment), search_tsv (full text), news_post.tags (array overlap)
BRIN on created_at / published_at — append-only time columns, ~1000x smaller than a B-tree
PARTIAL on outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL — the only genuinely hot scan in the system

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: 4 · Why PostgreSQL — and explicitly why not the alternatives

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: A database choice is only defensible next to the options it beat. Decision record: ADR-0001, revisit trigger = p95 primary CPU > 60% for 7 days.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: The shape of the domain fits it.
Roughly 90% of this system is relational with hard integrity rules; the remaining 10% (spec sheets,
page blocks, UTM payloads, ATS answers) is document-shaped. Postgres is the only mainstream engine
that is genuinely first class at both. JSONB + GIN gives you MongoDB's flexibility without giving up
joins, foreign keys or transactions — so the flexibility argument for Mongo simply disappears.
The one thing that must not break is transactional.
A dropped enquiry is lost revenue. lead + lead_item + outbox must commit or fail as a unit. ACID gives
that in a single statement, with no distributed-transaction machinery and no dual-write race.
It absorbs the next three roadmap features without introducing a new datastore:
full-text search -> tsvector + pg_trgm, good to ~10^5 docs, so OpenSearch is deferred not required
dealer / install map -> PostGIS radius and nearest-neighbour queries
'similar products', AI -> pgvector embeddings alongside the row they describe
cabinet IoT telemetry -> TimescaleDB hypertables in the same instance
One engine to operate, back up, monitor, tune and hire for. That is the real cost saving.
Read scaling here is boring and proven.
Streaming read replicas + PgBouncer absorb a 100x read spike, and 95% of reads never reach the
database because the CDN already answered. Writes are in the hundreds per day — a single primary is
the correct answer for years, and saying so is part of the design, not an omission.
Logical decoding + Debezium turns every commit into an event for search, cache purge and the
warehouse. Combined with the outbox table this removes the dual-write bug class entirely.
It is cheap, portable, and hard to get locked into.
RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Neon, Supabase or a plain VM — same SQL, same dump. The exit cost is a
pg_dump, which is exactly the property you want in a vendor decision you cannot yet justify revisiting.
Limits we accept, with the mitigation written down:
single writer (fine at this write volume) · vacuum and bloat need monitoring · connection cost needs
PgBouncer · major-version upgrades need a rehearsed blue/green drill. All standard, all in the runbook.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: The catalogue is a graph with integrity rules, not a pile of documents. Orphaned variants and dangling asset references
are the number-one CMS bug class and Mongo cannot express the constraint that prevents them. $lookup is weak and slow
for the faceted admin queries this team runs daily, and multi-document transactions remain a bolt-on. Its one genuine
advantage — schemaless specs — is already covered by JSONB + GIN with joins left intact. Choosing it here means
hand-rolling referential integrity in application code forever.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Excellent when every access pattern is known up front and write scale is unbounded. We have neither. 'Products where
capacity > 600 L and refrigerant = R290, faceted by industry' is ad-hoc by nature, and the BI team needs joins. You
would pay in GSI sprawl, denormalisation and write-amplification for a workload of tens of writes per day. Right tool,
wrong problem — and no SQL for analytics.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: MySQL / Aurora MySQL — viable, not chosen

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: This would genuinely work; it is not a bad answer. What it costs: GIN-indexed JSON containment, tsvector ranking,
ltree, PostGIS, pgvector, exclusion constraints, and Debezium-grade logical decoding. Every one of those is already on
the roadmap (specs, search, breadcrumbs, dealer map, semantic search, CDC). Pick MySQL only if the team's existing ops
muscle is MySQL — that reason beats this list.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Firestore / Airtable / Sheets as the backend — rejected

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Firestore: weak ad-hoc querying, per-read billing that punishes a crawler walking the catalogue, no SQL for BI, heavy
lock-in. Airtable or Sheets is genuinely tempting at 350 SKUs and will work for a quarter, then deliver no
transactions, no referential integrity, hard API rate limits and no migration path. Supabase is fine — but it *is*
Postgres, so that is a hosting decision, not a database decision.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch as the primary store — rejected

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: No transactions, no foreign keys, painful and lossy on mapping changes, and a reindex bug becomes permanent data loss
rather than a cache miss. Its correct role is a derived, disposable index fed by CDC — which is exactly how it appears
in layer 6. The same reasoning excludes Redis-as-database.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Headless SaaS CMS alone (Contentful / Sanity) — partially adopted

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Superb editor experience for pages and news, and worth paying for. But product specs, RFQ leads and CV applications
need our own transactional store, real joins and our own retention and erasure controls — and per-record SaaS pricing
across 350 SKUs x N locales is poor value. Chosen middle path: Payload or Strapi running on OUR Postgres. One schema,
one backup, one restore drill, and the editors still get a good CMS.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: 5 · Scaling path — buy the next 10x, not the next 1000x

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Each phase is triggered by a metric, never by a calendar date. Premature distribution is the most expensive mistake available here.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Hand-written HTML + CSS on a CDN.
HOLDS: a handful of pages, content
changed by a developer in git.
BREAKS WHEN: a non-developer has to
publish, or SKUs pass roughly 30, or
the same spec appears on 4 pages and
they start to disagree with each other.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Next.js on Vercel or Cloud Run.
Payload CMS on the SAME Postgres.
No Redis, no Kafka, no mesh.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Still ONE codebase; the services in
Capacity check: a 40 rps expo spike
is one replica and a warm cache. The
work here is correctness and freshness,

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Extract only the seams that hurt, in
pgvector for the AI spec assistant.
TRIGGERS, not dates: p95 primary CPU
>60%, deploy lead time >1 day, or two

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: 6 · Capacity, SLOs and the risks worth building against

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Capacity — sized from reality, not vanity

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: TRAFFIC A B2B refrigeration brand in India lands around
Trade-show or campaign peak: 20-40 rps for a couple of hours.
With 95%+ CDN offload the origin sees under 2 rps even at peak.
One small instance and one replica is genuinely enough.
Hundreds of writes per day. A single primary is correct.
STORAGE 350 SKUs x (8 images x 300 KB + 2 PDFs x 3 MB) ~ 8 GB in S3.
Postgres stays under 2 GB, so the entire working set fits in RAM.
No sharding, ever, at this scale. Anyone proposing it is designing
for their promotion packet rather than for this business.
THE REAL BILL IS EGRESS Images dominate cost and LCP alike. AVIF plus
exact-width srcset plus immutable long-cache cuts it by roughly 70%,
which is why the image CDN in layer 2 is not a nice-to-have.

text.tspan: the lead endpoint gets the tighter target because it is
the only revenue-carrying write in the system.
LATENCY TTFB p75 < 400 ms · internal API p99 < 300 ms
WEB VITALS LCP p75 < 2.0 s · INP < 200 ms · CLS < 0.1
enforced by Lighthouse CI budgets — a regression fails
the build rather than quietly shipping. CWV is a Google
ranking input, so this is an SEO control, not polish.
DURABILITY RPO 5 min (WAL ship) · RTO 30 min, drilled quarterly
leads: zero tolerance -> outbox + DLQ + alert on depth > 0
FRESHNESS publish -> live p95 < 30 s · index lag p95 < 60 s
A11Y / SEO WCAG 2.2 AA with axe clean in CI · schema.org Product,
301 map maintained on every information-architecture change
ERROR BUDGET 0.1%/month ~ 43 min. Budget exhausted -> feature freeze
and the next sprint is reliability work. Not negotiable.

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: Top risks and what we actually build for them

text.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
text.tspan: 1 SEO REGRESSION ON MIGRATION — the existing URLs are the asset, and a
rebuild is the single most common way to lose organic traffic.
Build: crawl and freeze the current URL inventory, redirect table
loaded into edge KV, pre-launch diff of titles / canonicals /
structured data, staged traffic rollout with rank monitoring.
2 SILENT LEAD LOSS — invisible and expensive.
Build: synthetic end-to-end lead probe every 5 min, alert on zero
leads in a business hour, DLQ depth alarm, weekly DB-vs-CRM reconcile.
Build: Turnstile + honeypot + per-IP buckets; dealer pricing behind an
authenticated scope from phase 3 rather than public HTML.
4 IMAGE BLOAT FROM MARKETING UPLOADS — the usual cause of a slow site.
Build: the Media service enforces max dimensions, generates AVIF/WebP
variants, rejects anything over 8 MB, emits a blurhash placeholder.
5 SINGLE-WRITER POSTGRES IS A SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE.
Build: multi-AZ with automatic failover, PgBouncer reconnect, and a
read-only degraded mode so the catalogue keeps serving from cache
even while the primary is being replaced.
Build: ship as a container and keep the DB plain Postgres, so leaving
is a weekend of work rather than a rewrite.
